subject: Physics
title: Arjun's Radio Adventure: The Invisible Messenger
hook: Arjun builds a radio receiver and discovers the hidden waves that carry music across the city.

slides.title: Electromagnetic Waves: The Invisible Messenger
slides.storyContext: Arjun sits on his Mumbai apartment balcony, tuning an old radio. Static crackles, then suddenly a cricket commentary booms through the speaker. 'Where is this sound coming from?' he wonders. 'It's not a wire... it's flying through the air!' His teacher Kavya smiles. 'That's an electromagnetic wave, Arjun. Let's trace its journey.'

image.alt: Electromagnetic Waves: The Invisible Messenger — Electromagnetic Waves

slides.title: Setting the Scene
slides.storyContext: Arjun lives in a city where radio broadcasts, mobile signals, WiFi, and TV signals fill the air invisibly. Every day, billions of waves carry information—cricket scores, Bollywood songs, news in Hindi and English—from towers to his radio, unseen. Kavya has challenged him: 'Build a simple radio tuner and explain how it catches one specific station from the electromagnetic chaos around you.' Arjun decides to understand the physics behind this magic.

image.alt: Setting the Scene — Electromagnetic Waves

slides.title: What is an Electromagnetic Wave?
slides.storyContext: Kavya pulls out a diagram at her kitchen table. 'Imagine two dancers—Electricity and Magnetism. They dance perpendicular to each other, both perpendicular to the direction they're moving. That's an EM wave, Arjun. Neither electricity nor magnetism alone, but both oscillating together, pushing the wave forward at light speed.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: An electromagnetic wave is a self-propagating oscillation of electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and to the direction of motion.

points.label: Key Property
points.text: All EM waves travel at speed c = 3 × 10^8 m/s in vacuum, regardless of frequency or wavelength.

points.label: Why No Medium?
points.text: Unlike sound (which needs air or water), EM waves can travel through empty space because they don't vibrate a physical medium—they ARE oscillating fields.

example.problem: A radio wave has a frequency of 100 MHz. What is its wavelength?
example.solution: c = f × λ. λ = c / f = (3 × 10^8 m/s) / (100 × 10^6 Hz) = 3 m. The wavelength is 3 meters, which is why AM radio requires reasonably tall antennas.

slides.inSimpleWords: An EM wave is electricity and magnetism doing a synchronized dance through space at the speed of light, needing no medium to carry it.

image.alt: What is an Electromagnetic Wave? — Electromagnetic Waves

slides.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
slides.storyContext: Vikram, the local radio broadcaster, invites Arjun to the studio. On the wall is a chart showing a rainbow of invisible waves. 'See,' Vikram points, 'your eyes see only a tiny slice—visible light. But our radio signal here is far below. A TV signal is here. Cell towers broadcast at these frequencies. And above visible light, X-rays and gamma rays from space. It's all the same phenomenon, just different frequencies.'

points.label: Spectrum Order (low to high frequency)
points.text: Radio waves → Microwaves → Infrared → Visible light → Ultraviolet → X-rays → Gamma rays

points.label: Relation: c = f × λ
points.text: Lower frequency = longer wavelength. Higher frequency = shorter wavelength, higher energy.

points.label: Radio Waves
points.text: f ~ 10^3 to 10^10 Hz, λ ~ 10^5 to 10^-2 m. Used for AM/FM radio, TV, WiFi, mobile phones.

points.label: Visible Light
points.text: f ~ 4–8 × 10^14 Hz, λ ~ 400–700 nm. Only this range our eyes detect.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electromagnetic waves come in many frequencies and wavelengths. Radio waves are low-frequency and long-wavelength; visible light is high-frequency and short-wavelength; all are the same underlying phenomenon.

image.alt: The Electromagnetic Spectrum — Electromagnetic Waves

slides.title: Maxwell's Equations & Wave Equation
slides.storyContext: Kavya shows Arjun a famous picture of James Clerk Maxwell. 'He unified electricity and magnetism mathematically, Arjun. His four equations predict that changing electric and magnetic fields create each other, forming a self-sustaining wave that races through space. This was theoretical in 1865—no one had made a radio yet. But it was so elegant that physicists believed it before experiments proved it.'

points.label: Maxwell's Key Insight
points.text: A changing electric field induces a magnetic field. A changing magnetic field induces an electric field. This mutual induction allows waves to exist.

points.label: Wave Equation
points.text: For E-field: ∂²E/∂t² = c² ∇²E. Solution: E = E₀ sin(kx - ωt), where k = 2π/λ (wave number) and ω = 2πf.

points.label: Phase Relationship
points.text: E and B oscillate in phase (zero phase difference) and are perpendicular in space.

example.problem: An EM wave has amplitude E₀ = 100 V/m and frequency f = 50 MHz. Write the equation for the electric field and find the amplitude of the magnetic field.

slides.inSimpleWords: Maxwell showed that electricity and magnetism create each other in a feedback loop, and this loop propagates as a wave at light speed. No wires needed—just empty space.

image.alt: Maxwell's Equations & Wave Equation — Electromagnetic Waves

slides.title: Polarization & Energy Transport
slides.storyContext: Arjun adjusts the radio antenna—vertical, horizontal, diagonal. 'Why does the signal strength change with angle?' he asks. Kavya smiles. 'The antenna responds to the electric field's oscillation direction. If the wave is polarized vertically and your antenna is horizontal, you get poor reception. That's polarization, Arjun. Also, EM waves carry energy—that's why the radio heats up slightly near strong transmitters.'

points.label: Polarization
points.text: The direction of the electric field oscillation. Linear polarization: E vibrates in one fixed plane. Can be vertical, horizontal, or at any angle.

points.label: Energy Density
points.text: u = (1/2)(ε₀ E² + B²/μ₀). Both electric and magnetic components carry energy equally.

points.label: Poynting Vector
points.text: S = (1/μ₀) E × B (cross product). Magnitude S = EB/μ₀. Points in direction of energy flow, measured in W/m².

points.label: Intensity
points.text: I = <S> = (1/2μ₀c) E₀² = (ε₀c/2) E₀². Average energy flux.

example.problem: An EM wave has E₀ = 500 V/m. Calculate the intensity of the wave.
example.solution: I = (ε₀c/2) E₀² = (8.85 × 10^-12 × 3 × 10^8 / 2) × (500)² = (1.33 × 10^-3) × 250000 = 332.5 W/m². This is the average power per unit area carried by the wave.

slides.inSimpleWords: Polarization is the direction in which the electric field wiggles. Waves carry energy in the direction they travel, measurable as intensity (power per unit area).

image.alt: Polarization & Energy Transport — Electromagnetic Waves

slides.title: Worked Example: Radio Antenna Design
slides.storyContext: Vikram wants to broadcast a new FM station at 101.5 MHz and asks Arjun for antenna advice. 'For maximum efficiency, the antenna should be about half the wavelength of the broadcast signal. What length antenna do I need?'

example.problem: Design an antenna for an FM broadcast at 101.5 MHz. (a) Find the wavelength. (b) What antenna length captures the wave most efficiently? (c) The transmitter outputs 5 kW. At a distance of 1 km, what is the intensity of the wave?
example.solution: (a) λ = c/f = (3 × 10^8 m/s) / (101.5 × 10^6 Hz) ≈ 2.96 m. (b) Half-wavelength antenna: L = λ/2 ≈ 1.48 m. (c) Power spreads over a sphere of radius 1 km: Area = 4πr² = 4π × (10^3)² ≈ 1.26 × 10^7 m². Intensity = Power / Area = 5000 W / (1.26 × 10^7 m²) ≈ 3.97 × 10^-4 W/m² ≈ 0.4 mW/m². This matches typical FM receiver sensitivity.

image.alt: Worked Example: Radio Antenna Design — Electromagnetic Waves

slides.title: Challenge: Microwave Oven Power
slides.storyContext: Arjun's mother uses a microwave to heat rice. 'Why doesn't it heat the plate but heats the food?' he wonders. The answer: microwaves have f ≈ 2.45 GHz (λ ≈ 12 cm), which match the resonance of water molecules. Arjun's challenge: calculate the photon energy and explain why microwaves, not radio waves, heat food.

example.problem: A microwave oven operates at 2.45 GHz. (a) Find the wavelength. (b) Calculate the energy of one microwave photon using E = hf, where h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J·s. (c) Compare this to the energy of a visible light photon (f ≈ 5 × 10^14 Hz). Why do microwaves heat but visible light doesn't?
example.solution: (a) λ = c/f = (3 × 10^8) / (2.45 × 10^9) ≈ 0.122 m ≈ 12.2 cm. (b) E_microwave = hf = (6.63 × 10^-34) × (2.45 × 10^9) ≈ 1.62 × 10^-24 J ≈ 1.01 × 10^-5 eV. (c) E_visible = (6.63 × 10^-34) × (5 × 10^14) ≈ 3.32 × 10^-19 J ≈ 2 eV. Microwave photons are ~10^5 times lower energy. However, microwaves heat because their wavelength (~12 cm) resonates with water molecule rotations, not because of photon energy alone. Visible light is absorbed poorly by water. Microwaves deliver many low-energy photons efficiently.

image.alt: Challenge: Microwave Oven Power — Electromagnetic Waves

slides.title: Recap: Electromagnetic Waves
slides.storyContext: Arjun now tunes his radio with confidence. Kavya asks him to summarize what he's learned. He takes a breath and explains:

points.text: EM waves are oscillating electric and magnetic fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation.
All EM waves travel at c = 3 × 10^8 m/s in vacuum, related by c = f × λ.
The EM spectrum spans radio waves (low f, long λ) to gamma rays (high f, short λ).
Maxwell's equations unified electricity and magnetism, predicting EM waves theoretically.
EM waves carry energy (Poynting vector S = E × B / μ₀) and can be polarized.
Practical applications: radio, TV, WiFi, microwaves, medical imaging, telecommunications.

image.alt: Recap: Electromagnetic Waves — Electromagnetic Waves

subject: Physics
title: Priya's Eye: How Light Bends
hook: Priya's glasses have stopped working. To get them fixed, she must understand why lenses bend light and how her eye focuses.

slides.title: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments: Seeing the World Clearly
slides.storyContext: Priya's spectacles fog up as she enters the eye doctor's clinic on a humid Mumbai afternoon. Dr. Sharma hands her a pair of lenses. 'Before I give you new glasses, do you know how they work?' Priya shakes her head. 'Light bends when it passes through glass—refraction. Today, I'll teach you why, using nothing but geometry and one simple law.'

image.alt: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments: Seeing the World Clearly — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: The Mystery of Blurred Vision
slides.storyContext: Priya has worn glasses since class 8. Her friends tease her about 'four-eyes,' but she's learned to ignore them. At school today, a new experiment in physics class fascinates her: the teacher uses a convex lens to focus sunlight onto paper, burning a hole. 'That's the same lens,' the teacher says, 'that makes words in a book clear for myopic eyes.' Priya connects the dots: her lens bends light to form clear images on her retina. When the focusing isn't right, images blur. Dr. Sharma has challenged her: 'If you understand the math, I'll let you design your own lens strength.'

image.alt: The Mystery of Blurred Vision — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: Snell's Law & Refraction
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma dips a stick halfway into a glass of water at the clinic. 'Look, Priya, it appears bent even though the stick is straight. Light bends at boundaries between materials. This bending is refraction, and it obeys a simple law discovered 400 years ago.'

points.label: Snell's Law
points.text: n₁ sin(θ₁) = n₂ sin(θ₂), where n is the refractive index (measure of how much a material slows light), θ is the angle from the normal (perpendicular to the surface).

points.label: Refractive Index
points.text: n = c / v, where c = light speed in vacuum (3 × 10^8 m/s), v = light speed in medium. For air, n ≈ 1. For glass, n ≈ 1.5. Higher n means slower light, more bending.

points.label: Normal
points.text: The line perpendicular to the surface. Angles θ₁ and θ₂ are measured from the normal, not the surface.

example.problem: Light enters a glass lens (n = 1.5) from air (n = 1) at an angle of 30° from the normal. What is the angle of refraction in the glass?
example.solution: n_air × sin(θ_air) = n_glass × sin(θ_glass). 1 × sin(30°) = 1.5 × sin(θ_glass). 0.5 = 1.5 × sin(θ_glass). sin(θ_glass) = 1/3 ≈ 0.333. θ_glass ≈ 19.47°. The light bends toward the normal, bending closer to the vertical as it enters the denser medium.

slides.inSimpleWords: When light crosses from one material to another (like air to glass), it bends. The denser the material, the slower light travels in it, the more it bends.

image.alt: Snell's Law & Refraction — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: Thin Lens Equation & Magnification
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma shows Priya a diagram of a lens. 'A convex lens is like two refracting surfaces back-to-back. When parallel light rays hit it, they converge to a focus. For a thin lens, there's one beautiful formula that connects object distance, image distance, and focal length.'

points.label: Lens Equation
points.text: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, where f is focal length, u is object distance (positive if real), v is image distance (positive if real, negative if virtual).

points.label: Focal Length
points.text: f is the distance from lens to the point where parallel rays converge (for convex) or appear to diverge from (for concave). Shorter f means stronger lens.

points.label: Magnification
points.text: m = v / (-u) = image height / object height. Positive m: upright. Negative m: inverted. |m| > 1: magnified. |m| < 1: diminished.

points.label: Sign Convention
points.text: Real objects/images (on standard side): positive distances. Virtual (on opposite side or behind mirror/lens): negative distances.

example.problem: A book is placed 20 cm from a converging lens with focal length f = 10 cm. Where is the image formed? Is it real or virtual? What is the magnification?
example.solution: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v. 1/10 = 1/20 + 1/v. 1/v = 1/10 - 1/20 = 1/20. v = 20 cm. Image is real (v > 0), formed 20 cm on the opposite side. m = -v/u = -20/20 = -1. Image is inverted, same size as object. This is the setup for a movie projector.

slides.inSimpleWords: A thin lens formula tells where an image forms based on how far the object is from the lens. The magnification tells if it's bigger, smaller, or the same size.

image.alt: Thin Lens Equation & Magnification — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: Optical Instruments: Eye & Microscope
slides.storyContext: Priya studies the anatomy chart on Dr. Sharma's wall. The eye is a marvel of optics: cornea and lens focus light onto the retina (like a camera sensor). 'Your myopia, Priya, means your eyeball is slightly too long or your lens too strong. Light focuses in front of the retina, and far objects blur. My glasses correct this by placing a diverging lens in front of your eye—it spreads the rays just enough so they refocus on the retina.'

points.label: Normal Eye (Emmetropia)
points.text: Relaxed: focal length matches eye length (~2.5 cm). Distant objects form sharp images on retina. Near point (closest focus): ~25 cm. Far point: infinity.

points.label: Myopia (Short-sightedness)
points.text: Eye too long or cornea too curved. Distant rays focus in front of retina. Correction: diverging lens (concave, negative f).

points.label: Hyperopia (Long-sightedness)
points.text: Eye too short. Rays would focus behind retina. Correction: converging lens (convex, positive f).

points.label: Microscope
points.text: Two converging lenses: objective (short f, near object) forms real magnified image; eyepiece (short f) acts as magnifying glass. Total magnification = m_obj × m_eye.

slides.inSimpleWords: The eye is an optical system that focuses light. Defects in focus cause myopia or hyperopia, corrected by lenses. A microscope uses two lenses to magnify tiny objects.

image.alt: Optical Instruments: Eye & Microscope — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: Mirrors: Reflection & Focal Length
slides.storyContext: Ramesh, Priya's classmate, shows her a curved mirror in the science lab. 'Reflection is simpler than refraction,' he says. 'Light bounces off a mirror following one rule: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection. But a curved mirror focuses light like a lens does.'

points.label: Law of Reflection
points.text: θ_incident = θ_reflected, both measured from the normal to the surface.

points.label: Concave Mirror (Converging)
points.text: Reflects light toward a focus. Focal length f is positive. Mirror equation: same as lens, 1/f = 1/u + 1/v.

points.label: Convex Mirror (Diverging)
points.text: Reflects light away from focus. Focal length f is negative. Used for wide-angle rear-view mirrors.

points.label: Focal Length of Curved Mirror
points.text: f = R / 2, where R is radius of curvature.

example.problem: An object is placed 30 cm from a concave mirror with focal length f = 10 cm. Find the image position, nature, and magnification.
example.solution: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v. 1/10 = 1/30 + 1/v. 1/v = 1/10 - 1/30 = 2/30 = 1/15. v = 15 cm. Image is real, inverted, formed 15 cm in front of mirror. m = -v/u = -15/30 = -0.5. Image is half the size (diminished) and inverted. This is used in makeup mirrors and searchlights.

slides.inSimpleWords: Curved mirrors focus light via reflection, following the same mirror equation as lenses. Concave mirrors converge; convex mirrors diverge.

image.alt: Mirrors: Reflection & Focal Length — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: Worked Example: Telescope Design
slides.storyContext: Priya visits a planetarium in her city and sees the telescope. 'How do astronomers see so far into space?' she wonders. An enthusiast explains: 'A telescope also uses two lenses—exactly like a microscope, but arranged for distant objects. The objective collects faint light from stars, and the eyepiece magnifies. Let me show you the math.'

example.problem: A telescope has an objective lens with focal length f_obj = 100 cm and an eyepiece with focal length f_eye = 5 cm. (a) What is the angular magnification? (b) If the eye of an observer has a near point of 25 cm, what should be the tube length L (distance between lenses) for normal adjustment (image at infinity)?
example.solution: (a) Angular magnification M = f_obj / f_eye = 100 / 5 = 20. The telescope magnifies 20×. (b) For normal adjustment (relaxed eye viewing at infinity), the eyepiece forms a virtual image at infinity. This requires the intermediate real image from the objective to be at the focal point of the eyepiece. Tube length L = f_obj + f_eye = 100 + 5 = 105 cm. A 20× telescope needs a tube about 1 meter long.

image.alt: Worked Example: Telescope Design — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: Challenge: Designing Priya's New Glasses
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma gives Priya a project. 'Your near point is 40 cm instead of 25 cm due to myopia. I need to prescribe a lens such that you can read a book 25 cm away. The lens should also let you see distant objects clearly. What power (in diopters) do I need?'

example.problem: Priya's near point is 40 cm. She wants to read at 25 cm. She also needs to see distant objects. (a) What focal length lens corrects her vision for distance (infinity)? (b) For reading (25 cm), using the lens from part (a), where does the image form? (c) Power of lens in diopters: P = 1/f (in meters). Calculate P.
example.solution: (a) Myopia is corrected by a diverging lens (f < 0) that makes the infinity-image land on her retina. For a myopic person whose far point (unaided) is D_far (say 2 m), the correction is f = -D_far. Without knowing D_far precisely, we use: for myopia with near point 40 cm, a typical correction might be f ≈ -0.5 m to -0.67 m. Let's assume f = -0.5 m (example). (b) With the lens: using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with u = -0.25 m (virtual object, since the book is now closer than the near point wants), 1/(-0.5) = 1/(-0.25) + 1/v gives 1/v = -2 + 4 = 2, so v = 0.5 m. But this requires careful refitting. (c) P = 1/|f| = 1/0.5 = 2 diopters (negative power: -2 D for a diverging lens).

image.alt: Challenge: Designing Priya's New Glasses — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: Recap: Ray Optics & Optical Instruments
slides.storyContext: Priya puts on her new glasses—crisp prescription, perfectly ground—and reads without strain for the first time in weeks. Dr. Sharma asks her to recap the lesson:

points.text: Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ governs refraction at material boundaries.
Thin lens equation: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v relates object distance, image distance, and focal length.
Magnification: m = -v/u tells us if images are magnified, diminished, upright, or inverted.
The human eye is an optical system; myopia and hyperopia are focusing errors, corrected by diverging and converging lenses.
Mirrors obey the same equation as lenses; concave mirrors converge, convex mirrors diverge.
Optical instruments (microscopes, telescopes, magnifying glasses) combine lenses to magnify objects.

image.alt: Recap: Ray Optics & Optical Instruments — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

subject: Physics
title: Aditya's Interference Dream
hook: Aditya sees oil on a puddle shimmer with rainbow colors. His teacher reveals it's interference—proof that light is a wave.

slides.title: Wave Optics: Light as a Wave
slides.storyContext: Aditya notices an oil puddle outside his Mumbai coaching center, lit by morning sun. The surface is a kaleidoscope of reds, greens, violets. 'It's soap film interference,' says Prof. Nair, who happens to pass by. 'Two waves of light reflect off the top and bottom of the oil layer. Depending on the thickness, they can add up (bright) or cancel (dark). This is wave optics—where light shows its wave nature.'

image.alt: Wave Optics: Light as a Wave — Wave Optics

slides.title: Two Sides of Light
slides.storyContext: For centuries, Newton believed light was made of particles. But in class 12 physics, Aditya learns a shocking fact: light sometimes acts like particles (photons), sometimes like waves. Today's experiments use the wave model. Prof. Nair challenges him: 'If light is a wave, two light waves should interfere—they should add when in phase, cancel when out of phase. Find proof in the lab, and you'll have unlocked a secret Isaac Newton missed.'

image.alt: Two Sides of Light — Wave Optics

slides.title: Interference: Coherence & Path Difference
slides.storyContext: Leela sets up a ripple tank in the lab. Two dippers vibrate, creating waves that interact. 'See where the crests meet crests—constructive interference, big waves. Where crests meet troughs—destructive interference, calm water,' Leela explains. 'Light does the same. Two coherent light sources create an interference pattern.'

points.label: Constructive Interference
points.text: Path difference = nλ, where n = 0, 1, 2, ... Two waves crest-to-crest: amplitude adds. Intensity I = 4I₀ (for equal amplitudes).

points.label: Destructive Interference
points.text: Path difference = (2n+1)λ/2. Two waves crest-to-trough: amplitudes cancel. Intensity I = 0 (for equal amplitudes).

points.label: Coherence
points.text: For stable interference, sources must have same frequency (monochromatic) and constant phase relationship. Ordinary light sources are incoherent; lasers are coherent.

points.label: Condition for Visibility
points.text: Paths must differ by < coherence length (for light, ~few micrometers, thus need nearly monochromatic light).

example.problem: Two coherent light sources emit light of wavelength λ = 500 nm. At a point, the path difference is 1500 nm. Is it constructive or destructive interference?
example.solution: Path difference = 1500 nm = 3 × 500 nm = 3λ. Since 3 is an integer, this is constructive interference. Intensity is maximum.

slides.inSimpleWords: When two light waves overlap, they interfere: if crests align, they add (bright); if crest meets trough, they cancel (dark). This proves light is a wave.

image.alt: Interference: Coherence & Path Difference — Wave Optics

slides.title: Young's Double-Slit Experiment
slides.storyContext: Prof. Nair dims the lab lights and shows a classic setup: a laser, two slits cut in a screen, and a white wall beyond. A striped pattern of bright and dark lines appears. 'This is Young's experiment from 1801, Aditya. Monochromatic light passes through two slits. Each slit acts as a coherent source. On the wall, you see interference fringes. From the fringe spacing, we can measure the wavelength of light. Extraordinary.'

points.label: Setup
points.text: Light of wavelength λ from a source passes through two slits S₁, S₂ separated by distance d. Light is observed on a screen at distance D away (D >> d).

points.label: Path Difference
points.text: At a point P on screen, distance y from center: Δ = (d × y) / D (for small angles).

points.label: Bright Fringe
points.text: Δ = nλ. Spacing between adjacent bright fringes: Δy = λD / d. Smaller d or larger λ → wider fringes.

points.label: Dark Fringe
points.text: Δ = (n + 1/2)λ. Dark fringes are midway between bright fringes.

example.problem: In a double-slit setup, λ = 600 nm, d = 1 mm, D = 1 m. Find the distance between the central bright fringe (n=0) and the first bright fringe (n=1).
example.solution: Distance between adjacent bright fringes: Δy = λD / d = (600 × 10^-9 × 1) / (1 × 10^-3) = 0.6 × 10^-3 m = 0.6 mm. The first bright fringe is 0.6 mm from the center.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light passing through two slits creates an interference pattern of bright and dark lines. The fringe spacing reveals the wavelength of light.

image.alt: Young's Double-Slit Experiment — Wave Optics

slides.title: Diffraction: Light Bends Around Obstacles
slides.storyContext: Aditya looks at a light bulb through a fine-mesh cloth. The light spreads into a grid of bright and dark squares—diffraction. 'When light meets an obstacle or slit comparable to its wavelength, it bends around it. This is diffraction,' Leela explains. 'It's a consequence of wave nature. Particles don't diffract; waves do.'

points.label: Single-Slit Diffraction
points.text: Light passes through a single slit of width a. Waves from different parts of the slit interfere. Dark fringes appear at angles θ where a sin(θ) = nλ (n = 1, 2, 3, ...).

points.label: Central Maximum
points.text: Bright central fringe is twice as wide as side maxima. Most of diffracted light energy is here.

points.label: Intensity Pattern
points.text: I = I₀ [sin(β) / β]², where β = (πa sin θ) / λ. Maxima when β ≈ 1.43π, 2.46π, ...

points.label: Diffraction vs. Interference
points.text: Both are wave phenomena. Diffraction: single slit/obstacle. Interference: multiple coherent sources.

slides.inSimpleWords: When light passes through a narrow opening or around an obstacle, it bends and spreads. This diffraction is proof of light's wave nature.

image.alt: Diffraction: Light Bends Around Obstacles — Wave Optics

slides.title: Polarization & Optical Activity
slides.storyContext: Leela hands Aditya two pieces of polaroid film. When she stacks them, light passes through. When she rotates one 90°, darkness. 'Light waves oscillate perpendicular to their direction of travel. Normally, all directions are equal (unpolarized). Polaroid filters only allow oscillations along one axis. If two filters are perpendicular, no light gets through.'

points.label: Linear Polarization
points.text: E-field oscillates in one fixed plane. Polaroid filters absorb components perpendicular to their transmission axis.

points.label: Malus's Law
points.text: If light is polarized and passes through a polarizer, I_transmitted = I₀ cos²(θ), where θ is angle between polarization and polarizer axis.

points.label: Brewster's Angle
points.text: At angle θ_B = tan^(-1)(n₂/n₁), reflected light is fully polarized perpendicular to plane of incidence. tan(θ_B) = n_glass / n_air ≈ 1.5.

points.label: Optical Activity
points.text: Some substances (sugar, quartz, amino acids) rotate the plane of polarized light. Angle of rotation: θ = αℓ, where α is specific rotation, ℓ is path length.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light waves can be polarized (oscillations restricted to one direction). Polaroid filters, Brewster's angle reflection, and optically active substances demonstrate this.

image.alt: Polarization & Optical Activity — Wave Optics

slides.title: Worked Example: Measuring Wavelength with Diffraction Grating
slides.storyContext: In the advanced lab, Aditya uses a diffraction grating—a device with thousands of parallel slits. 'Each slit is a coherent source. The grating separates light by wavelength. Let me show you how to measure λ precisely.'

example.problem: Light passes through a diffraction grating with 1000 lines/mm. The first-order diffraction maximum (m=1) for a spectral line appears at an angle of 20°. Find the wavelength.
example.solution: Grating spacing: d = 1 / (1000 lines/mm) = 1 × 10^-6 m = 1 μm. Grating equation: d sin(θ) = mλ. For m=1, θ=20°: λ = d sin(20°) / 1 = 1 × 10^-6 × 0.342 ≈ 342 nm. This is in the ultraviolet range, suggesting this could be a cadmium or mercury spectral line.

image.alt: Worked Example: Measuring Wavelength with Diffraction Grating — Wave Optics

slides.title: Challenge: Oil Film Colors
slides.storyContext: Aditya returns to the puddle with oily film. 'Why are the colors arranged in rings and why do they change when I look from different angles?' Using thin-film interference, he works out the answer.

example.problem: A thin film of oil (refractive index n = 1.4) floats on water. Light of wavelength λ = 550 nm (in air, yellow-green) is incident normally. For constructive interference at the film surface (considering both reflections and phase change), what is the minimum thickness of the film?
example.solution: For a thin film with air above and water below: reflection at air-oil interface introduces a π phase shift (denser medium), reflection at oil-water interface has no π shift (less dense to more dense). Net phase difference from path = (2nt) × (2π/λ₀), where t is thickness, n is refractive index of oil. Adding the π shift from reflection: for constructive interference, 2nt = (m - 1/2)λ₀ (m = 1, 2, ...). Minimum: m = 1: t = λ₀ / (4n) = 550 × 10^-9 / (4 × 1.4) = 550 / 5600 × 10^-9 ≈ 98 nm. This is about 0.1 micrometers, confirmed by optical observations of oil films.

image.alt: Challenge: Oil Film Colors — Wave Optics

slides.title: Recap: Wave Optics
slides.storyContext: Aditya writes up his lab report. Prof. Nair reviews it with satisfaction. 'You've shown that light is truly a wave. The colors in soap films, the stripes in Young's double-slit, the spreading of light through a slit—all wave phenomena. Newton would be amazed.' Aditya smiles and closes his notebook:

points.text: Interference: Two coherent light waves add constructively (bright) or destructively (dark) depending on path difference.
Young's double-slit: Creates a striped pattern; fringe spacing β = λD/d reveals wavelength.
Diffraction: Light bends around obstacles or through slits; single slit produces dark fringes at a sin θ = nλ.
Polarization: Light's E-field can oscillate in a specific direction; polarizers, Brewster's angle, and optical activity show this.
Thin-film interference: Oil films, soap bubbles, and anti-reflection coatings use constructive/destructive interference.
Wave optics explains phenomena particle models cannot: Newton's rings, diffraction gratings, the photoelectric effect (partially).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
title: Rohan's Quantum Leap: When Light Behaves Like Particles
hook: Rohan's phone has a photoelectric cell. Pushing it toward a red lamp doesn't trigger it, but a blue lamp does. Why?

slides.title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter: A Quantum Revolution
slides.storyContext: Rohan sits in Dr. Banerjee's quantum physics office, holding a smartphone with a broken camera sensor—it's being replaced because it's sensitive to only short-wavelength light (blue, UV) and not red. 'Your phone uses the photoelectric effect,' Dr. Banerjee explains. 'Light isn't just a wave; in 1905, Einstein showed it's also made of particles—photons. Each photon carries energy E = hf. Only photons energetic enough (high frequency) can knock electrons free from metal. Red light's photons are too weak. That's why your sensor fails with red light.'

image.alt: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter: A Quantum Revolution — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: Particles of Light & the Photoelectric Mystery
slides.storyContext: For over a century, the wave model of light explained everything—interference, diffraction, polarization. But experiments in the early 1900s showed something strange: when light hits metal, electrons are ejected (photoelectric effect). The puzzle: no matter how bright red light is, it never ejects electrons. But even dim blue light ejects them instantly. 'This makes no sense,' Dr. Banerjee says, 'if light is purely a wave. Brighter light = more energy, so red should work.' Rohan gasps: 'Unless light is made of particles—photons—and each photon carries energy depending on frequency, not intensity.'

image.alt: Particles of Light & the Photoelectric Mystery — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: Photon Energy & Einstein's Photoelectric Equation
slides.storyContext: Dr. Banerjee writes on the board: E = hf. 'Planck discovered this in 1900. h is a tiny constant (6.63 × 10^-34 J·s, Planck's constant). Higher frequency light = higher photon energy. A metal surface has a work function φ (minimum energy to eject an electron). If hf > φ, an electron escapes with kinetic energy KE_max = hf - φ. If hf < φ, no electron escapes, no matter how bright the light.'

points.label: Photon Energy
points.text: E = hf = hc/λ, where h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J·s, c = 3 × 10^8 m/s. Lower wavelength (higher frequency) = higher energy.

points.label: Work Function
points.text: φ is the binding energy of electrons to a metal (typically 2-5 eV for metals). Threshold frequency: f₀ = φ/h. Below this, no photoelectric effect.

points.label: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation
points.text: hf = φ + KE_max. Photon energy = work function + kinetic energy of ejected electron.

points.label: Stopping Potential
points.text: V_s = KE_max / e (in volts). A reverse voltage that stops even the fastest electron: eV_s = hf - φ.

example.problem: Zinc has a work function φ = 3.6 eV. Light of wavelength λ = 250 nm is incident. (a) Find the photon energy. (b) What is the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons? (c) What is the stopping potential?

slides.inSimpleWords: Light is made of photons, each carrying energy E = hf. The higher the frequency, the more energetic the photon. A photon hits metal and ejects an electron only if its energy exceeds the metal's work function.

image.alt: Photon Energy & Einstein's Photoelectric Equation — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: De Broglie Waves: Matter as Waves
slides.storyContext: Zara, an artist, asks Dr. Banerjee: 'If light acts like matter (particles), can matter act like light (waves)?' Dr. Banerjee smiles. 'In 1924, Louis de Broglie proposed exactly that. Every particle—electron, proton, even a cricket ball—has an associated wavelength λ = h/p, where p is momentum. The more massive the object, the shorter its wavelength. Electrons are light enough that their de Broglie wavelength is measurable. This is why electrons can be diffracted, proving they're waves too.'

points.label: De Broglie Wavelength
points.text: λ = h/p = h/(mv), where m is mass, v is velocity, h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J·s. For non-relativistic particles.

points.label: Wavelength of an Electron
points.text: At 1 eV kinetic energy, λ ≈ 1.2 nm (in UV range, measurable with crystalline diffraction). At 100 eV, λ ≈ 0.12 nm (X-ray range).

points.label: Diffraction of Matter
points.text: Electrons, neutrons, and even atoms diffract through slits or off crystal planes, proving their wave nature. Used in electron microscopes.

points.label: Dual Nature
points.text: Photons and matter are both wave and particle: wave nature in propagation and interference; particle nature in energy and momentum exchanges.

example.problem: An electron is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. (a) Find its kinetic energy in eV. (b) Calculate its momentum. (c) Find its de Broglie wavelength.
example.solution: (a) KE = eV = 100 eV. (b) Momentum: KE = p²/(2m), so p = sqrt(2m × KE) = sqrt(2 × 9.11 × 10^-31 × 100 × 1.6 × 10^-19) = sqrt(2.9 × 10^-48) ≈ 5.4 × 10^-24 kg·m/s. (c) λ = h/p = (6.63 × 10^-34) / (5.4 × 10^-24) ≈ 1.23 × 10^-10 m = 0.123 nm. This is in the X-ray region, and matches experimental electron diffraction data.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electrons, like light, have a dual nature. They have a wavelength λ = h/p (de Broglie wavelength), which is why they can be diffracted and interfere like waves.

image.alt: De Broglie Waves: Matter as Waves — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: Compton Effect: Photon-Electron Scattering
slides.storyContext: Dr. Banerjee describes an experiment: X-rays (high-frequency photons) scatter off electrons. The scattered X-rays have a slightly longer wavelength than the incident rays. 'This is impossible if photons are purely waves. But if photons are particles with momentum p = E/c = h/λ, then scattering is an elastic collision between a photon and an electron. The electron recoils, taking energy, so the photon exits with less energy and longer wavelength.'

points.label: Compton Scattering
points.text: High-frequency photon hits electron at rest. Electron recoils; photon scatters with reduced frequency (longer wavelength).

points.label: Wavelength Shift
points.text: Δλ = λ' - λ = (h/m_e c) (1 - cos θ), where θ is scattering angle, m_e is electron mass, h/m_e c ≈ 2.43 × 10^-12 m (Compton wavelength).

points.label: Compton Wavelength
points.text: λ_C = h/(m_e c) ≈ 2.43 pm (picometers). For 90° scattering, wavelength shift = λ_C.

points.label: Energy & Momentum Conservation
points.text: Before: photon E = hf, momentum p = E/c. After: photon E' = hf', electron KE and momentum. Totals conserved.

slides.inSimpleWords: When a photon collides with an electron, it scatters and loses energy, emerging with a longer wavelength (lower frequency). This proves photons carry momentum.

image.alt: Compton Effect: Photon-Electron Scattering — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: Bohr Model & Quantized Energy Levels
slides.storyContext: Rohan asks: 'If electrons are waves, why don't they spiral into the nucleus? Why are atoms stable?' Dr. Banerjee explains: 'Niels Bohr in 1913 proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus in specific quantized orbits, where the electron's de Broglie wavelength fits perfectly around the orbit. An electron can only be in these allowed orbits; transitions between orbits emit or absorb photons of specific energies, producing spectral lines.'

points.label: Bohr's Quantization Condition
points.text: 2πr = nλ_dB = nh/(mv), where n = 1, 2, 3, ... Only certain radii are allowed.

points.label: Orbital Radius (Hydrogen)
points.text: r_n = (n²/Z) × a₀, where a₀ = 0.53 Å (Bohr radius), Z = atomic number. For hydrogen, r₁ = 0.53 Å, r₂ = 2.1 Å, etc.

points.label: Energy Levels (Hydrogen)
points.text: E_n = -13.6 eV / n². For n=1 (ground state), E₁ = -13.6 eV. For n=2, E₂ = -3.4 eV. E_∞ = 0 (ionized).

points.label: Photon Emission
points.text: Transition from n_i to n_f emits photon: hf = E_i - E_f = 13.6 (1/n_f² - 1/n_i²) eV.

example.problem: An electron in hydrogen jumps from n=2 to n=1 (Lyman alpha line). Find the energy and wavelength of the emitted photon.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electrons in atoms are confined to specific energy levels. They can jump between levels by absorbing or emitting photons. This explains atomic spectra.

image.alt: Bohr Model & Quantized Energy Levels — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: Worked Example: Photoelectric Effect Experiment
slides.storyContext: Rohan sets up a photoelectric experiment in the lab. He shines light of different wavelengths on a zinc plate and measures the stopping potential (reverse voltage that stops all photoelectrons).

example.problem: Light of wavelength 300 nm is incident on zinc (φ = 3.6 eV). (a) Is photoelectric effect observed? (b) If yes, find the stopping potential. (c) What is the threshold wavelength for zinc?
example.solution: (a) E_photon = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10^-34 × 3 × 10^8) / (300 × 10^-9) = 6.63 × 10^-19 J = 4.14 eV. Since 4.14 eV > 3.6 eV, yes, photoelectric effect occurs. (b) KE_max = 4.14 - 3.6 = 0.54 eV. Stopping potential V_s = 0.54 V. (c) Threshold: hf₀ = φ, so λ₀ = hc/φ = (6.63 × 10^-34 × 3 × 10^8) / (3.6 × 1.6 × 10^-19) = 3.45 × 10^-7 m = 345 nm. Light must be ≤ 345 nm.

image.alt: Worked Example: Photoelectric Effect Experiment — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: Challenge: Electron Microscope Resolution
slides.storyContext: Rohan learns that an electron microscope can resolve features smaller than a light microscope. The reason: electron de Broglie wavelength is much shorter than visible light. A transmission electron microscope (TEM) operates at 100 kV. What is the electron wavelength, and how much better is the resolution?

example.problem: In a TEM, electrons are accelerated through 100 kV. (a) Find the kinetic energy in joules. (b) Calculate the momentum and de Broglie wavelength. (c) Compare to visible light (λ ≈ 500 nm). What is the improvement factor?
example.solution: (a) KE = eV = 100 × 10^3 × 1.6 × 10^-19 = 1.6 × 10^-14 J. (b) From KE = p²/(2m), p = sqrt(2 × 9.11 × 10^-31 × 1.6 × 10^-14) ≈ 5.4 × 10^-22 kg·m/s. λ = h/p = (6.63 × 10^-34) / (5.4 × 10^-22) ≈ 1.23 × 10^-12 m = 0.00123 nm. (c) Improvement: 500 nm / 0.00123 nm ≈ 4 × 10^5 times smaller wavelength. This allows resolution of atomic structures, impossible with light microscopy.

image.alt: Challenge: Electron Microscope Resolution — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: Recap: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
slides.storyContext: Rohan closes his quantum notebook, understanding the revolution that reshaped physics. Light is not just waves; matter is not just particles. Both have dual nature, depending on the experiment. He tells Dr. Banerjee:

points.text: Light acts as particles (photons) with energy E = hf and momentum p = E/c.
Photoelectric effect: photons eject electrons from metal only if hf > φ (work function).
Matter acts as waves with de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p, allowing electrons to diffract and interfere.
Compton effect: photon-electron collisions conserve energy and momentum, confirming photon particle nature.
Bohr model: electrons are confined to quantized orbits where the de Broglie wavelength fits. Transitions emit/absorb photons with specific energies.
Dual nature is fundamental: the same entity behaves differently depending on how we measure it.

image.alt: Recap: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

subject: Physics
title: Sneha's Atomic Mystery: Inside the Nucleus
hook: Sneha watches uranium decay in the lab and asks: why do atoms split? What holds the nucleus together?

slides.title: Atoms: The Nucleus & Nuclear Forces
slides.storyContext: Sneha stands at the glass of a nuclear physics lab at Mumbai's research center, watching a Geiger counter click rapidly as it nears a sealed uranium sample. 'What's inside the nucleus that makes it unstable?' she asks Prof. Desai. 'Protons and neutrons held by the strong nuclear force—stronger than electromagnetism at short range, but complex. Today, we'll map the atom's nucleus, explore binding energy, and ask: why do some nuclei burst apart?'

image.alt: Atoms: The Nucleus & Nuclear Forces — Atoms

slides.title: The Rutherford Scattering Experiment
slides.storyContext: Prof. Desai recounts a historic experiment from 1909: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, under Rutherford's direction, fired alpha particles (helium nuclei) at thin gold foil. Most passed straight through. But a few bounced back, as if hitting a hard wall. 'Rutherford was stunned,' Prof. Desai says. 'He concluded the atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense nucleus at its center—like planets orbiting the sun, but with the nucleus repelling alpha particles electromagnetically. This proved the nuclear model of the atom.'

image.alt: The Rutherford Scattering Experiment — Atoms

slides.title: Nuclear Structure: Protons, Neutrons, Mass Number
slides.storyContext: Sneha studies a chart showing nuclei. 'Every nucleus is made of protons (positive charge) and neutrons (neutral). Protons define the element—carbon always has 6 protons. But the number of neutrons can vary, creating isotopes.'

points.label: Atomic Number Z
points.text: Number of protons. Determines chemical identity. Z_H = 1, Z_C = 6, Z_U = 92.

points.label: Mass Number A
points.text: Total number of nucleons (protons + neutrons). Denoted by superscript, e.g. C-12 means A=12 (6 protons + 6 neutrons).

points.label: Isotopes
points.text: Same element (same Z), different mass numbers (different A). Example: C-12, C-13, C-14 are carbon isotopes.

points.label: Nuclear Radius
points.text: R ≈ 1.2 × A^(1/3) fm (femtometers, 10^-15 m). Nucleus is ~10^-15 m, atom is ~10^-10 m. Nucleus is 100,000 times smaller than atom, yet contains 99.9% of mass.

example.problem: Uranium-238 has Z=92. (a) How many protons? (b) How many neutrons? (c) Estimate the nuclear radius.
example.solution: (a) 92 protons (defines uranium). (b) Neutrons = A - Z = 238 - 92 = 146. (c) R ≈ 1.2 × (238)^(1/3) ≈ 1.2 × 6.2 ≈ 7.4 fm (femtometers).

slides.inSimpleWords: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons. Protons determine what element it is. Neutrons add mass. The nucleus is tiny but dense, containing virtually all the atom's mass.

image.alt: Nuclear Structure: Protons, Neutrons, Mass Number — Atoms

slides.title: Binding Energy & Mass Defect
slides.storyContext: Prof. Desai shows Sneha an astonishing result. 'Take hydrogen-1: 1 proton + 1 neutron = deuterium (heavy hydrogen). Add up their individual masses and you get slightly MORE than the nucleus's actual mass. The difference—the mass defect—has been converted into binding energy holding the nucleus together. E = mc².'

points.label: Mass Defect
points.text: Δm = Z × m_p + (A-Z) × m_n - M_nucleus, where m_p ≈ 1.00728 u, m_n ≈ 1.00866 u, 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c².

points.label: Binding Energy
points.text: B = Δm × c² (in energy units). B is the energy released when nucleons are assembled, or needed to disassemble the nucleus.

points.label: Binding Energy per Nucleon
points.text: B/A (in MeV/nucleon). Higher B/A means more stable nucleus. Fe-56 has maximum B/A ≈ 8.8 MeV/nucleon.

points.label: Nuclear Stability
points.text: Nuclei with B/A > 8.5 are stable. Light nuclei need equal protons & neutrons; heavy nuclei need more neutrons (Coulomb repulsion).

example.problem: Calculate the binding energy of He-4 (alpha particle): 2 protons + 2 neutrons. m_p = 1.00728 u, m_n = 1.00866 u, M_He4 = 4.0026 u, 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c².
example.solution: Δm = (2 × 1.00728) + (2 × 1.00866) - 4.0026 = 2.01456 + 2.01732 - 4.0026 = 0.0293 u. B = 0.0293 × 931.5 ≈ 27.3 MeV. Binding energy per nucleon: 27.3 / 4 ≈ 6.8 MeV/nucleon. (Alpha particles are very stable.)

slides.inSimpleWords: The nucleus is held together by binding energy, which corresponds to a small loss of mass (mass defect) via E = mc². Nuclei with high binding energy per nucleon are most stable.

image.alt: Binding Energy & Mass Defect — Atoms

slides.title: Radioactive Decay: Alpha, Beta, Gamma
slides.storyContext: Aryan points at the Geiger counter's clicks. 'Unstable nuclei spontaneously emit radiation—alpha particles, beta particles, or gamma rays—to reach a more stable configuration. The process is random; we can't predict when one nucleus will decay. But we can count how many decay in a given time, using the decay constant λ.'

points.label: Alpha Decay
points.text: Heavy nucleus emits He-4 nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons). A → A-4, Z → Z-2. Example: U-238 → Th-234 + He-4.

points.label: Beta-Minus Decay
points.text: Neutron converts to proton + electron (beta) + antineutrino. A stays same, Z → Z+1. Example: C-14 → N-14 + e + ν_bar.

points.label: Gamma Decay
points.text: Nucleus emits high-energy photon (gamma ray). No change in A or Z, just releases excess energy.

points.label: Activity & Half-life
points.text: N(t) = N₀ × (1/2)^(t/T_half). Activity A = λN (decays per second). λ = ln(2) / T_half.

example.problem: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years. (a) Find the decay constant λ. (b) If a sample starts with 1 mole (6.02 × 10^23 atoms), how many remain after 11,460 years?

slides.inSimpleWords: Radioactive nuclei spontaneously decay by emitting alpha, beta, or gamma radiation. The number of remaining nuclei halves every half-life period.

image.alt: Radioactive Decay: Alpha, Beta, Gamma — Atoms

slides.title: Nuclear Fission & Fusion
slides.storyContext: Prof. Desai shows a diagram of uranium fission. 'A slow neutron hits U-235. The nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei (Ba-141, Kr-92, plus 2-3 free neutrons). The binding energy per nucleon increases, so mass is released as heat (E = mc²). This is fission, used in nuclear reactors and weapons. Fusion is the opposite: light nuclei combine (like hydrogen isotopes forming helium) in stars, also releasing energy.'

points.label: Fission Reaction
points.text: U-235 + neutron → Ba-141 + Kr-92 + 3 neutrons + 200 MeV. Each neutron can trigger more fissions (chain reaction).

points.label: Fusion Reaction
points.text: Deuterium + Tritium → He-4 + neutron + 17.6 MeV. Used in thermonuclear weapons, pursued for clean energy.

points.label: Energy Release
points.text: ΔE from mass defect: Δm × c². For fission of U-235: ~200 MeV per fission. 1 kg U-235 ≈ 82 TJ (terajoules).

points.label: Q-value
points.text: Q = (M_initial - M_final) c². Positive Q: exothermic (releases energy). Negative Q: endothermic (requires energy).

slides.inSimpleWords: Fission splits heavy nuclei into lighter ones, releasing energy. Fusion combines light nuclei into heavier ones, also releasing energy. Both obey E = mc².

image.alt: Nuclear Fission & Fusion — Atoms

slides.title: Worked Example: Dating with Carbon-14
slides.storyContext: Sneha asks: 'How do archaeologists date ancient artifacts?' Prof. Desai explains: 'Living organisms absorb C-14 (radioactive) and C-12 (stable) at a fixed ratio. When they die, they stop absorbing new C-14. The existing C-14 decays, lowering the ratio. By measuring this ratio today, we calculate how long ago the organism died.'

example.problem: A wooden artifact shows C-14 activity of 8 decays per minute per gram of carbon. Modern living wood shows 15.3 decays per minute per gram. Half-life of C-14 is 5,730 years. How old is the artifact?
example.solution: Activity ratio: A / A₀ = 8 / 15.3 ≈ 0.523. Using N ∝ A (for same sample), and N(t) = N₀ × (1/2)^(t/T), we have 0.523 = (1/2)^(t/5730). Taking log: log(0.523) = (t/5730) × log(0.5). -0.281 = -0.301 × (t/5730). t = 0.281 × 5730 / 0.301 ≈ 5,300 years. The artifact is approximately 5,300 years old.

image.alt: Worked Example: Dating with Carbon-14 — Atoms

slides.title: Challenge: Calculating Binding Energy
slides.storyContext: Sneha is tasked with calculating the binding energy of the most stable nucleus: Fe-56. Why is Fe-56 special? Its binding energy per nucleon is at a maximum.

example.problem: Fe-56: 26 protons, 30 neutrons. Atomic mass = 55.9349 u. (a) Calculate mass defect. (b) Find binding energy. (c) Binding energy per nucleon. (d) Compare to C-12 (B/A = 7.7 MeV/nucleon). (Given: m_p = 1.00728 u, m_n = 1.00866 u, 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c²)
example.solution: (a) Δm = (26 × 1.00728) + (30 × 1.00866) - 55.9349 = 26.189 + 30.260 - 55.935 = 0.514 u. (b) B = 0.514 × 931.5 ≈ 478.8 MeV. (c) B/A = 478.8 / 56 ≈ 8.55 MeV/nucleon. (d) This is higher than C-12's 7.7, confirming Fe-56's exceptional stability. Elements lighter than Fe fuse to gain energy; heavier elements fission.

image.alt: Challenge: Calculating Binding Energy — Atoms

slides.title: Recap: Atoms and Nuclear Physics
slides.storyContext: Sneha closes her nuclear lab notebook, having glimpsed the heart of matter. The nucleus, once thought indivisible, contains tremendous energy and follows laws as precise as those of planets and atoms. She tells Prof. Desai:

points.text: Nucleus contains protons (Z) and neutrons (A-Z). Nuclear radius R ≈ 1.2 A^(1/3) fm.
Binding energy B arises from mass defect via E = mc². Nuclei with maximum B/A (Fe-56) are most stable.
Radioactive decay (alpha, beta, gamma) occurs when nuclei transform to more stable configurations. N(t) = N₀(1/2)^(t/T).
Fission (heavy → light) and fusion (light → heavy) both release energy when ΔE = Δm × c².
Nuclear forces (strong interaction) dominate at 10^-15 m scale, balancing Coulomb repulsion.
Applications: energy production, medical imaging/therapy (PET, radiotherapy), dating, materials science.

image.alt: Recap: Atoms and Nuclear Physics — Atoms

subject: Physics
title: Karan's Fusion Dream: The Sun's Secret
hook: Karan learns the sun doesn't burn coal; it fuses hydrogen. He wonders: can we replicate the sun on Earth?

slides.title: Nuclei: Fusion, the Sun's Power, and the Future
slides.storyContext: Karan stands at the Mumbai Science Centre's planetarium, mesmerized by the sun's image. Dr. Malhotra appears beside him. 'The sun has burned for 4.6 billion years. Its fuel isn't coal—it's hydrogen. In the core, hydrogen fuses into helium, releasing the energy that lights Earth. The process is called nuclear fusion. Today, I'll teach you the physics of the sun and the dream of clean fusion power on Earth.'

image.alt: Nuclei: Fusion, the Sun's Power, and the Future — Nuclei

slides.title: The Sun's Furnace
slides.storyContext: Maya asks an urgent question: 'Climate change is real. Can we abandon fossil fuels?' Dr. Malhotra nods. 'Fusion is one answer. The sun fuses 600 million tons of hydrogen every second, converting mass to energy via E = mc². If we can harness this on Earth, we have infinite clean power.' Karan, fascinated, dives into the physics. 'Why hasn't fusion been achieved? What's the challenge?' Dr. Malhotra smiles. 'Temperature, pressure, and confinement. The sun's core is 15 million Kelvin. We need similar conditions in a lab—without the sun's gravity.'

image.alt: The Sun's Furnace — Nuclei

slides.title: Binding Energy & Nuclear Forces Revisited
slides.storyContext: Dr. Malhotra draws the binding-energy curve: a smooth hump peaking at iron-56. 'Light nuclei fusing upward and heavy nuclei splitting downward both move toward the hump's peak, releasing energy. Fusion of hydrogen to helium releases 26.7 MeV per reaction—a huge amount for a tiny mass.'

points.label: Strong Nuclear Force
points.text: Acts only at ~10^-15 m (nuclear scale). 100× stronger than electromagnetic. At longer range, E.M. repulsion dominates (why nuclei need neutrons).

points.label: Energy Curve
points.text: B/A peaks at Fe-56 (~8.8 MeV/nucleon). Moving toward Fe from either direction releases energy.

points.label: Fusion Path
points.text: H → He → C → ... → Fe releases energy. Fission path: U → ...→ Fe also releases energy.

points.label: Critical Mass & Coulomb Barrier
points.text: For nuclei to fuse, they must overcome Coulomb repulsion (energy ~10 MeV). In sun, some reactions tunnel through barrier at lower E due to quantum mechanics.

slides.inSimpleWords: The strong nuclear force binds nucleons together, balancing electromagnetic repulsion. Nuclei move toward iron-56 via fusion or fission, releasing energy.

image.alt: Binding Energy & Nuclear Forces Revisited — Nuclei

slides.title: The Proton-Proton Chain in the Sun
slides.storyContext: Dr. Malhotra shows the sun's primary fusion reaction: 'Four hydrogen nuclei (protons) fuse into one helium-4 nucleus. The pathway is called the proton-proton chain, or PP chain. It happens in three steps.'

points.label: Step 1
points.text: p + p → deuteron (d) + e+ + ν_e. Two protons fuse into a bound deuteron, releasing a positron and electron neutrino. Slowest step (~10 billion years per proton).

points.label: Step 2
points.text: d + p → He-3 + γ. Deuteron fuses with a proton, forming He-3 (light helium) and a gamma ray.

points.label: Step 3
points.text: He-3 + He-3 → He-4 + 2p. Two He-3 fuse into He-4, releasing two protons back into the cycle.

points.label: Net Reaction
points.text: 4p → He-4 + 2e+ + 2ν_e + γ. Four protons become one helium, releasing 26.7 MeV total. The sun fuses ~620 million tons/second.

example.problem: Calculate the mass defect for p + p + p + p → He-4 + 2e+. (m_p = 1.00728 u, m_He4 = 4.0026 u, m_e = 0.000549 u, 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c²).
example.solution: Δm = 4 × 1.00728 - (4.0026 + 2 × 0.000549) = 4.02912 - 4.004 ≈ 0.0251 u. E = 0.0251 × 931.5 ≈ 23.4 MeV (neglecting neutrino mass; actual is ~26.7 MeV accounting for positron annihilation with ambient electrons: e+ + e- → 2γ, releasing 1.02 MeV).

slides.inSimpleWords: In the sun's core, hydrogen fuses via a three-step chain reaction to form helium, releasing 26.7 MeV per reaction and powering the sun.

image.alt: The Proton-Proton Chain in the Sun — Nuclei

slides.title: Deuterium-Tritium Fusion on Earth
slides.storyContext: Karan asks: 'If the sun uses hydrogen, why can't we just copy the sun's reaction?' Dr. Malhotra shakes his head. 'The PP chain is too slow for a reactor. Instead, we use deuterium (heavy hydrogen) and tritium (superheavy hydrogen). Their Coulomb barrier is lower, so they fuse at lower temperatures. This is the most promising reaction for fusion reactors: d + t → He-4 + n + 17.6 MeV.'

points.label: Deuterium-Tritium Reaction
points.text: d + t → He-4 + n + 17.6 MeV. Cross-section peaks at ~65 keV, far lower than proton-proton (~keV average in sun).

points.label: Reaction Rate
points.text: σ(E) = effective cross-section. High at low E. At E = 10 keV (T~100 million K), σ_dt >> σ_pp.

points.label: Lawson Criterion
points.text: n × τ > 10^20 (S.I.), where n is particle density, τ is confinement time. Fusion gain (Q > 1) requires density and confinement products above this.

points.label: Energy Balance
points.text: Triple product (n, T, τ) determines efficiency. ITER (experimental reactor) aims for Q > 10; NIF (National Ignition Facility) achieved Q ≈ 1 in 2022.

slides.inSimpleWords: Deuterium-tritium fusion is easier than hydrogen fusion because the Coulomb barrier is lower. Reactors use DT reactions, but confinement remains the challenge.

image.alt: Deuterium-Tritium Fusion on Earth — Nuclei

slides.title: Confinement & Temperature Requirements
slides.storyContext: Maya asks: 'Why is fusion so hard?' Dr. Malhotra sighs. 'We need temperatures of 100+ million Kelvin to give nuclei enough kinetic energy to overcome Coulomb repulsion. At that temperature, matter is plasma—ions and free electrons. It expands, cools, and escapes. Confining it without losing energy is the bottleneck. Two methods: magnetic confinement (tokamaks) and inertial confinement (lasers).'

points.label: Temperature for Fusion
points.text: T ~ 10-100 million K (10-100 MK). At T=15 MK (sun's core), reaction rate is slow; at 100 MK (lab), faster.

points.label: Magnetic Confinement
points.text: Tokamak (doughnut-shaped reactor) uses strong magnetic fields (B ~ 5 Tesla) to trap plasma. Ions spiral along field lines, contained.

points.label: Inertial Confinement
points.text: NIF uses 192 laser beams to compress a fuel capsule to ~1000 times normal density in picoseconds. Inertia (not magnetic field) confines the reaction.

points.label: Energy Loss Mechanisms
points.text: Bremsstrahlung (radiation from electron-ion collisions), conduction, convection. Must minimize losses to achieve Q > 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fusion requires extreme temperature and density. Magnetic fields or laser compression can confine the plasma. The goal is to extract more energy than input.

image.alt: Confinement & Temperature Requirements — Nuclei

slides.title: Worked Example: Sun's Luminosity
slides.storyContext: Dr. Malhotra poses a classic question: 'The sun's luminosity is 3.8 × 10^26 watts. From the PP chain, each reaction releases 26.7 MeV. How many reactions per second occur in the sun?'

example.problem: Sun's luminosity L = 3.8 × 10^26 W. Each PP-chain reaction releases 26.7 MeV. (a) Convert MeV to joules. (b) How many reactions per second?
example.solution: (a) 26.7 MeV × 1.6 × 10^-13 J/MeV = 4.27 × 10^-12 J per reaction. (b) Reactions per second = L / energy per reaction = (3.8 × 10^26 W) / (4.27 × 10^-12 J) ≈ 8.9 × 10^37 reactions/s. At ~4 protons per reaction, ~3.6 × 10^38 protons fuse per second in the sun—equivalent to the sun converting ~600 million tons of hydrogen to helium every second.

image.alt: Worked Example: Sun's Luminosity — Nuclei

slides.title: Challenge: Achieving Fusion Gain
slides.storyContext: Karan wants to estimate what's needed for a fusion reactor to achieve Q=1 (energy out = energy in). Using the d-t reaction and Lawson criterion, can he find the required conditions?

example.problem: A fusion reactor aims for Q=1 using d-t fuel. Assume τ (confinement time) = 10 seconds, T = 100 million K. Use Lawson criterion n × τ ≥ 10^20 m^-3·s. (a) Find minimum particle density n. (b) If the reactor volume is 1000 m³, how many ions must be confined? (c) Estimate if this is realistic for a tokamak.
example.solution: (a) n ≥ 10^20 / τ = 10^20 / 10 = 10^19 m^-3 = 10^13 cm^-3. (b) Total ions ≈ 10^19 × 1000 = 10^22 ions. (c) Realistic tokamaks achieve n ~ 10^20 m^-3 and τ ~ 1 s, giving n×τ ~ 10^20, barely at Lawson limit. Improving τ or n further requires better confinement—the ongoing challenge in fusion research.

image.alt: Challenge: Achieving Fusion Gain — Nuclei

slides.title: Recap: Nuclei, Fusion, and Clean Energy
slides.storyContext: Karan and Maya leave the lab, energized by Dr. Malhotra's vision. He asks them to summarize what they've learned:

points.text: The sun's power comes from hydrogen fusion via the PP chain: 4p → He-4 + energy (26.7 MeV).
Fusion requires overcoming the Coulomb barrier. Temperatures of 10-100 million K are needed.
Earth-based reactors use deuterium-tritium fuel (17.6 MeV per reaction) because its barrier is lower.
Confinement is the bottleneck: magnetic (tokamak) or inertial (laser) methods trap plasma to prevent energy loss.
Lawson criterion n×τ ≥ 10^20 defines minimum density-time product for Q > 1 (energy-positive fusion).
Recent advances (NIF's Q ~ 1) suggest fusion energy is within reach. Clean, abundant power awaits.

title: Nikhil's Device Revolution: From Sand to Circuits
hook: Nikhil holds a smartphone and wonders: how do transistors shrink to nanometers and still work?

slides.title: Semiconductor Electronics: The Foundation of Modern Technology
slides.storyContext: Nikhil's phone contains billions of transistors. Mr. Gupta smiles. 'Silicon, one of the most abundant elements on Earth, has transformed civilization. By carefully mixing silicon with impurities, we create semiconductors—materials that conduct electricity when we want them to, and block it when we don't. This control is the basis of all modern electronics: phones, computers, solar cells, power supplies. Today, we'll reverse-engineer a transistor from first principles.'

image.alt: Semiconductor Electronics: The Foundation of Modern Technology — Semiconductor Electronics

slides.title: The Silicon Revolution
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta recounts: 'In the 1950s, the transistor replaced vacuum tubes. By the 1970s, integrated circuits packed thousands of transistors onto a silicon chip. Today, a smartphone has more transistors than stars in the galaxy—10+ billion on a single processor. The key innovation: doping—adding impurities (phosphorus, boron) to pure silicon to create p-type and n-type materials, forming junctions that switch electricity with precision and speed.' Nikhil's eyes widen as he realizes the entire digital world rests on controlled impurities in sand.

image.alt: The Silicon Revolution — Semiconductor Electronics

slides.title: Intrinsic & Extrinsic Semiconductors
slides.storyContext: Sophia explains: 'Pure silicon (intrinsic) has 4 valence electrons, forming covalent bonds with neighbors. At room temperature, few electrons break free (weak conduction). But add phosphorus (5 valence electrons, n-type doping), and the extra electron is weakly bound, easily freed—it becomes a mobile charge carrier. Add boron (3 valence electrons, p-type doping), and you create a "hole" (missing electron) that acts as a positive charge carrier. This is extrinsic silicon.'

points.label: Intrinsic Semiconductor
points.text: Pure silicon (Si). Four valence electrons, covalent bonding. Conductivity σ ∝ e^(-E_g/2kT), where E_g ≈ 1.1 eV (band gap).

points.label: N-type (Electron-doped)
points.text: Silicon + phosphorus (5 valence electrons). Extra electron is donor. E_d ≈ 0.05 eV below conduction band. At room T, most donors ionize, releasing free electrons.

points.label: P-type (Hole-doped)
points.text: Silicon + boron (3 valence electrons). Missing electron is acceptor (hole). E_a ≈ 0.05 eV above valence band. Holes are mobile positive charges.

points.label: Fermi Level
points.text: E_F is the energy level at which probability of occupation is 50%. In n-type, E_F closer to conduction band; in p-type, closer to valence band.

example.problem: At room temperature (T=300 K), intrinsic silicon has E_g = 1.1 eV. Estimate the fraction of electrons in the conduction band, assuming equal electron and hole densities n_i.
example.solution: n_i ∝ exp(-E_g / 2kT). kT at 300K ≈ 0.026 eV. -E_g / 2kT = -1.1 / 0.052 ≈ -21.2. n_i ∝ exp(-21.2) ≈ 6 × 10^-10. Very few charge carriers—intrinsic Si is a poor conductor. Doping increases carrier density by ~10 orders of magnitude.

slides.inSimpleWords: Pure silicon is a weak conductor. Doping it with phosphorus (n-type, extra electrons) or boron (p-type, holes) creates strong, controllable conductors.

image.alt: Intrinsic & Extrinsic Semiconductors — Semiconductor Electronics

slides.title: The P-N Junction & Diode Behavior
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta sketches a boundary between p-type and n-type silicon. 'Here's the magic: at the junction, electrons from n-type diffuse into p-type, recombining with holes. This creates a depletion region (charge imbalance). An electric field builds up, eventually stopping the diffusion. The junction acts like a one-way valve: forward bias (positive voltage on p-side) drives current; reverse bias blocks it.'

points.label: Depletion Region
points.text: Electrons and holes recombine at junction, leaving uncompensated donor and acceptor ions. Width W ~ 1 μm at typical doping.

points.label: Built-in Potential
points.text: V_bi = (kT/e) ln(N_A × N_D / n_i²). Typically 0.7 V for Si at room T. Opposes diffusion.

points.label: Forward Bias (V > V_bi)
points.text: External voltage reduces built-in potential. Electrons and holes inject across junction. Current rises exponentially: I = I_s (e^(V/V_T) - 1), where V_T = kT/e ≈ 26 mV at room T.

points.label: Reverse Bias (V < 0)
points.text: External voltage increases depletion width. Only thermally-generated charge carriers (leakage current) flow: I ≈ -I_s (constant, tiny).

example.problem: A silicon diode at 300 K has saturation current I_s = 10^-12 A. Find the current at V = 0.6 V forward bias and V = -5 V reverse bias.

slides.inSimpleWords: A p-n junction is a one-way valve for electric current. Forward bias conducts; reverse bias blocks. This is the basis of diodes.

image.alt: The P-N Junction & Diode Behavior — Semiconductor Electronics

slides.title: BJT (Bipolar Junction Transistor) & Amplification
slides.storyContext: Sophia introduces a three-terminal device: a BJT. 'Two p-n junctions back-to-back: collector-base (C-B) in reverse, base-emitter (B-E) in forward. A small current into the base controls a large current from collector to emitter. This is amplification. Gain (β) = I_c / I_b, typically 50-300.'

points.label: BJT Structure (NPN)
points.text: Three regions: emitter (n-type, high doping), base (p-type, thin, lightly doped), collector (n-type, moderate doping).

points.label: Active Mode
points.text: B-E junction forward biased, B-C reverse biased. Electrons from emitter diffuse through thin base into collector (most reach collector because base is thin).

points.label: Current Relationships
points.text: I_c ≈ β × I_b (β = current gain, 50-300). I_e = I_b + I_c. I_c is nearly independent of C-E voltage (in active region).

points.label: Saturation & Cutoff
points.text: Saturation: both junctions forward biased, current limited by resistances. Cutoff: both junctions reverse biased, I_c ≈ 0.

example.problem: An NPN BJT has β = 100. Base current I_b = 10 μA. Find collector current (active mode) and voltage drop across B-E junction.
example.solution: I_c = β × I_b = 100 × 10 × 10^-6 = 1 mA. Voltage drop across B-E in active mode (forward biased): V_BE ≈ 0.7 V for Si.

slides.inSimpleWords: A BJT is a three-terminal switch that amplifies: a tiny base current controls a large collector current. The gain is β, typically 50-300.

image.alt: BJT (Bipolar Junction Transistor) & Amplification — Semiconductor Electronics

slides.title: MOSFET: The Modern Transistor
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta shows a MOSFET (Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor). 'This is the workhorse of modern chips. Instead of base current, a voltage on the gate controls current between source and drain. No gate current flows (gate is insulated), so energy efficiency is superb. Billions of MOSFETs fit on a chip because they're tiny and consume minimal power.'

points.label: MOSFET Structure
points.text: Gate (metal electrode) separated from silicon by thin oxide insulator (~1-2 nm). Source and drain are heavily doped regions in substrate.

points.label: Operation (NMOS)
points.text: Apply positive gate voltage → electric field attracts electrons, forming an inversion layer (conductive channel) between source and drain. No gate current flows (insulated).

points.label: Key Advantage
points.text: No gate current → very low power consumption. Can be miniaturized (gate length now ~5 nm). Fast switching (picosecond timescales).

points.label: Threshold Voltage V_T
points.text: Gate voltage needed to form channel. Typically 0.3-0.7 V. Below V_T, device is off (nearly zero drain current).

slides.inSimpleWords: A MOSFET is a voltage-controlled switch. A voltage on the gate controls current between source and drain without consuming gate current. Ideal for integrated circuits.

image.alt: MOSFET: The Modern Transistor — Semiconductor Electronics

slides.title: Worked Example: Logic Gate (NAND) Design
slides.storyContext: Sophia explains how transistors build logic gates. 'Two NMOS transistors in series, pulling down to ground, with a resistor pulling up to positive supply. When both gates are high (+V), both transistors conduct, pulling output low (0). Otherwise, output stays high (1). This is a NAND gate.'

example.problem: Design an NAND gate with two NMOS transistors. Supply voltage = 5 V. Threshold voltage V_T = 0.5 V. When both inputs are 5 V, transistors conduct with on-resistance R_on ≈ 1 kΩ each. (a) Estimate pull-down resistance (series): R_pd. (b) If pull-up resistor is 10 kΩ, find output voltage when both inputs are 0 V.
example.solution: (a) R_pd = 2 × 1 kΩ = 2 kΩ (series). (b) When inputs are 0 V, both transistors are off (gate voltage < V_T). Output voltage ≈ V_cc × R_open / (R_open + R_pullup) ≈ 5 V (output is high). When both inputs are 5 V, pull-down dominates, output ≈ 0 V.

image.alt: Worked Example: Logic Gate (NAND) Design — Semiconductor Electronics

slides.title: Challenge: Solar Cell as Photodiode
slides.storyContext: Nikhil asks: 'How do solar panels work?' Mr. Gupta explains: 'A solar cell is a p-n junction exposed to sunlight. Photons knock electrons from the valence band to the conduction band, creating electron-hole pairs in the depletion region. The built-in electric field separates them: electrons to the n-side, holes to the p-side. This generates voltage and current without any external power.'

example.problem: A silicon solar cell receives photons of wavelength λ = 500 nm (green light). (a) Find photon energy. (b) If E_g = 1.1 eV, can this photon create an electron-hole pair? (c) For solar irradiance of 1000 W/m² and cell area 100 cm², estimate maximum current if each photon creates one charge carrier (assuming 80% of photons with E > E_g are absorbed).
example.solution: (a) E_photon = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10^-34 × 3 × 10^8) / (500 × 10^-9) ≈ 4 × 10^-19 J ≈ 2.5 eV. (b) Yes, 2.5 eV > 1.1 eV. (c) Number of photons: Power / energy = 1000 / (2.5 × 1.6 × 10^-19) ≈ 2.5 × 10^21 photons/s on 0.01 m² = 2.5 × 10^19 photons/s·cm². With 80% absorption: 2 × 10^19 electron-hole pairs/s = 2 × 10^19 C/s = 20 A (open circuit current density ~40 A/cm² typical for Si cells, so this order-of-magnitude estimate is reasonable).

slides.title: Recap: Semiconductor Electronics
slides.storyContext: Nikhil holds his phone again, now understanding the cascade of physics beneath the screen. He tells Mr. Gupta and Sophia:

points.text: Semiconductors (Si, Ge) have a band gap E_g. Doping with donors (n-type) or acceptors (p-type) creates mobile charge carriers.
P-N junction: built-in electric field creates a one-way valve. Forward bias conducts; reverse bias blocks. Basis of diodes.
BJT (Bipolar Junction Transistor): small base current controls large collector current (amplification). Gain β ~ 50-300.
MOSFET (Field Effect Transistor): gate voltage controls source-drain current with zero gate current. Ideal for low-power, high-density circuits.
Logic gates: MOSFETs arranged as pull-down/pull-up networks create NAND, NOR, inverters, building all digital logic.
Solar cells: p-n junctions exposed to light, converting photons to electricity via photoelectric effect in the depletion region.
